sections.html:
Waterbury is a New Haven County city, 33 miles southwest of Hartford and 77 miles northeast of New York City. It had 114,403 residents in 2020 and covers about 28.95 square miles along the Naugatuck River valley, with Interstate 84 and Route 8 meeting downtown. The "Brass City" nickname comes from the factories that once made it a national center for brass, clocks and silverware, and plenty of the older housing grew up around them.

Twenty-five recognized neighborhoods make up the city, among them Brooklyn, Bunker Hill, Hillside, the East End, Overlook, Town Plot, Washington Hill, Fairmount, Hopeville, Waterville, Pine Hill, Long Hill, Country Club, Crownbrook, Robinwood, Bucks Hill, the North End, South End, West Side and WOW (Walnut-Orange-Walsh). The assessor's records show how your parcel is valued compared with others near it.

sections.h2: The 2022 revaluation and the phase-in choice
sections.html:
Waterbury finished a state-mandated five-year revaluation for the October 1, 2022 Grand List, and the new values went into use for the budget year that began July 1, 2023. Residential values rose much faster than commercial ones, so many homeowners saw higher bills even though the mill rate fell.

The city had to choose between full implementation and a phase-in of up to five years. Its planning figures were about 40 mills for full implementation and a proposed 55.50 mills for a five-year phase-in. Those were estimates made ahead of the budget vote, not the rate on your bill, so ask the Tax Collector for the rate that actually applies.

A phase-in affects only increases. A decrease in assessed value is not phased in, and the Board of Aldermen can end a phase-in early. If you are buying or selling, ask whether any phase-in still touches the parcel.

The Assessor's Office appraises property at market value as of the last revaluation date and assesses it at the state-mandated 70 percent ratio. It also processes exemption applications and answers questions about how a given assessment was set.

  • Veteran exemption: requires a recorded DD214 and at least 90 days of wartime service. Record it before October 1 to receive it on the next bill.
  • Disabled veteran exemption: a Benefits Payment Statement is due before October 1.
  • Additional low income veteran exemption: apply between February 1 and October 1, and renew every two years.
  • Elderly and totally disabled homeowners program: applications run from February 1 to May 15.
  • Blind and 100 percent disability exemptions.

The office is on the courtyard level of 235 Grand Street. The main number is (203) 574-6821, and the exemption and renters' rebate line is (203) 574-6827.

Owners of rented property, other than residential property of up to six units where the owner lives, must return the annual income and expense report before June 1 or face a 10 percent penalty on the assessment.

Real estate tax is due in two halves. The city mails bills in late June, and the Tax Collector sends no separate bill for the second installment. Payment has to be made within a month of the due date, and after that interest runs from the due date. Not receiving a bill does not cancel the tax or the interest, under Connecticut General Statutes 12-130 and 12-146.

InstallmentDue dateLate interest
First halfJuly 11.5 percent per month after one month, from the due date, minimum $2.00 per bill
Second halfJanuary 1, no bill mailedSame rate and minimum

The 1.5 percent a month works out to 18 percent a year. The Tax Collector is at 235 Grand Street on the first floor, (203) 574-6810, with a real estate line at (203) 574-6815, open Monday to Friday from 9:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Keep your tax receipts for 15 years.

sections.h2: State conveyance tax for a Waterbury seller
sections.html:
The seller of Waterbury real estate files the Connecticut conveyance tax return when the deed is recorded. The Department of Revenue Services requires Form OP-236 for any price of $2,000 or more, and Waterbury's town code on the form is 151.

If the property is a principal residence and the price will not cover the mortgages and priority taxes and liens, a state exemption may apply. The same list covers a principal residence conveyed in lieu of foreclosure. Both can matter to an owner who owes more than a sale will bring.

Some state exemptions do not remove the municipal share, so ask your attorney or the town clerk what remains to be paid.

A tax balance does not block a sale. The unpaid tax and interest are taken from your proceeds at closing, and the closing attorney works from a written payoff from the Tax Collector. Because interest builds month by month from the due date, a payoff letter should be fresh. Ask for one close to the closing date.

  1. Phone the Tax Collector and ask what is owed on each installment.
  2. Ask for the payoff in writing, with a date it is good through.
  3. Tell your attorney about any other lien or mortgage on the house.
  4. At the closing table, check that the tax figure on the settlement statement matches the letter.

A cash buyer pays from the same proceeds and uses the same payoff process, so being behind on tax does not rule that route out.

If your bill jumped, the first call is to the Assessor's Office at (203) 574-6821, not the Tax Collector, who only bills and collects. Ask how your value was set, what the last revaluation date was and whether a phase-in applies. Bring recent sales of similar houses in your neighborhood and notes on any condition problems the assessor may not have seen.

Ask about exemptions at the same time. Many of them need an application by a set date each year, and a missed deadline can mean waiting for the next bill.

faqs.q: When are Waterbury real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half is due July 1 and the second half January 1. The city mails one bill in late June and sends no bill for the second installment.

faqs.q: What interest does Waterbury charge on late taxes?
faqs.a: Payment must be made within a month of the due date. After that, interest is 1.5 percent a month, or 18 percent a year, from the due date, with a $2.00 minimum per bill.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Waterbury assessment?
faqs.a: Call the Assessor's Office at (203) 574-6821, on the courtyard level of 235 Grand Street. The Tax Collector handles bills at (203) 574-6810.

faqs.q: Does Waterbury assess property at full value?
faqs.a: No. Property is appraised at market value as of the last revaluation date and assessed at the state-mandated 70 percent ratio.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Waterbury house if I am behind on taxes?
faqs.a: Yes. The unpaid tax and interest are paid from the proceeds at closing, using a written payoff from the Tax Collector.
